title: How to re-engage buyers who stop responding after showings: a Mac follow-up plan
metaTitle: Re-engage buyers who stop responding after showings | Lazur
description: Buyers go quiet after showings? See why it happens, what silence costs, and free fixes you can use on your Mac today, with no tool to buy.
secondaryKeywords: buyers go silent after a showing
follow up with buyers after a showing

intro: To re-engage buyers who stop responding, send one short, specific message on the channel they actually use, then set a clear date to close the file. Silence after a showing often means the buyer is still deciding, comparing options, or stuck on one question you can answer. This guide covers what silence costs, why it happens, and fixes you can start today on a Mac, using tools you may already have.
tldr: Silence after a showing usually means the buyer is still deciding, not that they are gone.
Text is the channel buyers prefer most, so start there, then send the full recap by email.
Send a same-day recap with one specific question, not a generic check-in.
Track each buyer in a sheet with a next-touch date, and close the file on purpose when they stay silent.

blocks.text: Why buyers go quiet after a showing

A showing feels like progress to you. To the buyer, it is one step in a long search. Many buyers who stop replying are not rejecting you. They may still be comparing homes, waiting on a lender, or talking it over with a partner or a friend. Your job is to make the next reply easy, not to guess at the reason.
How long you have to re-engage a buyer

The NAR 2025 Profile puts the median buyer search at 10 weeks, based on transactions from July 2024 to June 2025. A buyer you met early in a search may still be looking weeks later. The same profile found that 56% of buyers said finding the right property was the hardest part of buying. If your buyer went quiet after a home that almost worked, the search is not over. It is looking for the next one.
Text is the channel buyers prefer

Zillow's 2026 Consumer Housing Trends report asked buyers who hired an agent how they want to be contacted. Text message came first at 43%, phone calls at 31%, and email at 11%. Those are stated preferences, not reply rates, and the page did not show a sample size. Still, the gap is wide enough to shape your first message.

The split changes with age. Zillow reports that buyers 18 to 29 prefer text at 49% and phone at 22%. Buyers 60 and older prefer phone at 46% and text at 34%. If an older buyer has gone quiet, a short call followed by a text that says you called often works better than a string of messages. Check your notes first, because the buyer may have told you how they want to be reached.
A worked example of a quiet buyer

Say you showed a buyer a few homes on Saturday. They liked one, but hesitated on the price. That evening you sent a recap email with every listing link and no question. By Tuesday there was no reply. On Wednesday you sent a text asking whether the price was the only issue. The buyer answered the same afternoon with a question about the school district.

The lesson is not that texts always win. The recap gave the buyer nothing to answer. The text gave them one easy question, and it pointed at the real problem. Write down the question that got the reply, then reuse its shape with the next buyer who goes quiet.
Mistakes that make silence last longer

The first mistake is the generic check-in. A message that says just checking in, or any updates, gives the buyer nothing to answer. Silence is the easiest reply, so that is what you get. The second mistake is sending everything by email. Email is the least preferred channel for buyers who hired an agent in Zillow's data, at 11%.

The third mistake is following up with no new information for weeks. Each message should carry a fact, a new listing, a price change, or one question. The fourth is never closing the loop. Without a close-out message, a dead file stays in your head and crowds out buyers who still want you. The fifth is pushing after a clear no. A clear no still tells you why the search changed.
Re-engage buyers in Gmail without sounding pushy

Start by turning on templates. In Chrome, open Gmail, click the gear icon, and choose See all settings > Advanced. Find Templates, select Enable, and click Save Changes at the bottom of the page. Write your recap once, then open the compose window, click More options (the three dots at the bottom), and choose Templates > Save draft as template.

blocks.title: Send the text first
blocks.text: Keep the text short, with one question. Put the full recap and the links in Gmail, so the buyer has something to review once they reply.

To schedule a follow-up, click the arrow beside Send and choose Schedule send. Pick a time that suits the buyer, not your inbox. To send from the compose window, press ⌘ Return. If you want a thread back on your screen later, hover over it, click Snooze, and pick the time you planned to chase.
Track every buyer in Google Sheets

Make one sheet with five columns: buyer, last contact, channel, next touch, and status. Use Data > Data validation to add a dropdown for status, with options such as still deciding, asked for time, and no reply. Type a next-touch date, or use =TODAY() plus the number of days you want to wait. The formula keeps the date moving forward without you doing math.

Then highlight overdue rows. Select the table, choose Format > Conditional formatting, and use a custom formula such as =$D2<=TODAY(). Pick a light fill color. Overdue buyers now stand out before you open your inbox, which is when a dropped buyer is easiest to miss.

blocks.caption: A simple tracker layout. Adjust the columns to match your business.

blocks.text: Keep the status column honest. Reasons such as still deciding, price, another agent, or timing show patterns after a few weeks. If the same reason keeps coming back, the problem may be your recap or your listings, not the buyer. Adjust those first.
Keep a buyer's listings in one Chrome tab group

Buyers often ask to see a listing again, and scattered tabs slow you down. In Chrome, right-click a tab and choose Add tab to new group. Name the group after the buyer. Keep their listings, your search, and your recap together. When the buyer replies, the whole file is one click away, and you do not have to rebuild it from memory.
When to close the file

Set a close-out date in your tracker before you send the first follow-up. On that date, send one close-out message. Keep it honest and short. Tell the buyer the search has paused, that the door is open, and that one reply will restart it. This keeps your list clean, and it respects the buyer's time.

blocks.title: Check client data rules first
blocks.text: Buyer names, incomes, and loan details are sensitive. Follow your brokerage's rules for client data before you paste it into any tool, including Lazur. If your employer limits which AI tools you may use, follow that limit, even when a shortcut would be faster.
Do you need a paid CRM for this

No. A Gmail template, a Google Sheet, and a Chrome tab group cover the routine in this guide. A paid CRM can send reminders and log calls for you. Follow Up Boss lists its Grow plan at $69 per user per month on monthly billing. Its pricing page describes web and mobile apps, and it does not mention a Mac app. Check the current help center before you assume one exists.
Buy a tool only after the routine above has run for a few weeks, and you know which step breaks. Otherwise you pay for a system you have not yet shaped to your own work.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It can circle a control you are looking for, guide you one click at a time, draft text, and dictate at the cursor when you hold fn. It does not click for you, and it does not send your messages. You make every send.

The useful way to use Lazur here is for the small jobs around the follow-up. Ask where Templates lives, have it explain a formula in your tracker, or dictate a showing note into the sheet. It cuts down on hunting through menus. It will not decide what a buyer needs to hear, and you still own that call.
Start with the next buyer on your list

Pick one buyer who went quiet this week. Send the short text, then set the next-touch date in your sheet. You do not need to rebuild your whole pipeline today. One clean follow-up teaches you more than a full set of templates you never use.

faq.question: How long should I wait before I follow up with a buyer who went quiet?
faq.answer: Wait long enough that your message does not feel like a nag. The NAR 2025 Profile puts the median buyer search at 10 weeks, so a quiet buyer may still be active. Use the next-touch date in your sheet rather than memory, and keep each message purposeful.

faq.question: Should I text or email a buyer after a showing?
faq.answer: Use text for the quick check, because Zillow found 43% of buyers who hired an agent prefer text, compared with 11% for email. Use email for the recap and for anything with links or documents you want on record.

faq.question: What do I say in a close-out message?
faq.answer: Say the search has paused, that you will close the file for now, and that one reply will restart it. Keep it short and warm. Do not add guilt, and do not ask three questions at once.

faq.question: Is it okay to close the file without a reply?
faq.answer: Yes, as long as you sent a clear message first and gave the buyer a way back in. Log the file as paused with the reason. You can reopen it the next time the buyer contacts you.

faq.question: Do I need Follow Up Boss or another CRM for this?
faq.answer: No. A Gmail template and a Google Sheet cover the routine. Follow Up Boss lists Grow at $69 per user per month on monthly billing, and its pricing page does not mention a Mac app. Check its help center before you assume a Mac app exists.

faq.question: Can Lazur send the follow-up for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur drafts and types text and guides you through each step. It does not click buttons or send messages for you. You read the draft, change anything you want, and send it yourself.

faq.question: What happens to my buyers' information when I use Lazur?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot are sent to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your brokerage's client data rules still apply, so check them first.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, but it is not available.

costs.title: Lost buyers you already worked to win
costs.text: A showing costs you time, fuel, and some of the buyer's trust. A buyer who goes quiet after a good showing may still buy, but from someone who kept talking. You do not get a second first impression. Silence after a showing can quietly turn a warm lead into a closed file.

costs.title: A pipeline that looks fuller than it is
costs.text: Every quiet buyer still sits on your list as active. That makes your forecast look better than it is, and it makes your week harder to plan. When you cannot tell a stalled buyer from a busy one, you spend time on the wrong calls. The fix is a status column that tells the truth.

costs.title: Repeat business you are not earning
costs.text: The NAR 2025 Profile found that more than 9 in 10 buyers would use their agent again. That loyalty is worth protecting. A buyer who feels forgotten after a showing has less reason to call you back. Silence costs you the next deal as well as this one.

costs.title: Deals that fall apart in the open
costs.text: Redfin counted just over 53,000 canceled purchase agreements nationwide in September 2025. Those are formal cancellations, so they say little about silent buyers. They do show how often deals fail between an offer and a closing, which is why steady contact through the process matters.

causes.title: They are still deciding
causes.text: NAR's 2025 Profile found that 56% of buyers said finding the right property was the hardest part of buying. A buyer who has not found a home they trust may stall rather than say no. Silence in that case is a pause. Your recap should help them decide, not just remember the homes you showed.

causes.title: Buyer's remorse or doubt after the showing
causes.text: Inman quoted Redfin agent Jo Chavez as saying, 'I'm seeing a lot of buyer's remorse.' That comment was about contract cancellations, but the same doubt can cool a showing. A buyer who starts to second-guess the price or the neighborhood may stop replying while they think it through.

causes.title: Money or job worries
causes.text: Inman's coverage lists failed negotiations and economic worries as reasons buyers back out, and it mentions buyers worried about job security. A buyer worried about income may go quiet instead of saying no. A direct question about timing or budget gives them a low-pressure way to answer.

causes.title: The channel you chose is the wrong one
causes.text: Zillow found that text is the most preferred contact method for buyers who hired an agent, at 43%. Email came in at 11%. If your only follow-up is an email, you are using the channel buyers prefer least. Email still matters for the paper trail, so use it second.

causes.title: The buyer is talking to another agent
causes.text: Some buyers talk to more than one agent before they choose one. If your buyer has gone quiet, they may be interviewing someone else. You will not know unless you ask. A short, direct question about where things stand is kinder than guessing, and it gives you the answer you need.

causes.title: Your last message gave them nothing to answer
causes.text: A recap with no question, or a check-in with no new fact, leaves the buyer with nothing to do. Silence is the default reply to a message that asks for nothing. Add one specific question, and the next reply becomes an easy yes, no, or a short sentence.

fixes.title: Send a same-day recap with one question
fixes.text: Write a short recap while the showing is fresh. List the homes you saw, add one honest note on each, and end with one question. For example, ask which home felt closest to what they want and what they would change. A specific question gets a specific answer, and it tells you what to do next.

fixes.title: Text the short version, then email the full recap
fixes.text: Send a text first with the question. Then email the full recap with links, notes, and anything you want on record. The text carries the question, and the email is the paper trail. This pairs the channel buyers prefer with the record you need.

fixes.title: Ask a question with a short answer
fixes.text: Use closed questions for the first follow-up, such as: Is the budget still the same? Would a different area work better? Is there a home you want another look at? Each one has a clear reply. Save the open-ended questions for the phone call, when the buyer has time to talk.

fixes.title: Set a next-touch date and keep it
fixes.text: Put a date in the next-touch column the day you send a message. When the date arrives, the row shows up in your conditional formatting. Follow up on that date, even if the message is short. A kept date builds trust, and a forgotten one erodes it.

fixes.title: Call older buyers and leave a clear voicemail
fixes.text: Zillow reports that buyers 60 and older prefer phone at 46% and text at 34%. If the buyer's age or your notes point to calls, call once, then send a text that says you called. Keep the voicemail short and end with one question they can answer by text.

fixes.title: Name the reason for each silence
fixes.text: Write one reason in your tracker for every quiet buyer. Use simple words such as still deciding, price, timing, or another agent. After a few weeks, the pattern tells you whether to change your recap, your listings, or your pricing advice. Guessing does not teach you anything. Patterns do.

fixes.title: Send a close-out message that leaves the door open
fixes.text: When the date passes and the buyer has not replied, send one message. Say the search has paused, that you will close the file for now, and that one reply will restart it. This is honest, short, and easy to answer. It also lets you stop carrying the file in your head.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Send the recap
plan.text: The same day as the showing, send a text with one specific question about the homes you saw. Then email the full recap with links to each listing. Log both messages in your tracker.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Sort each buyer and note the reason
plan.text: Sort each quiet buyer into a group: replied, still deciding, asked for time, or no reply. Write the reason in one short line in the status column.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Send one follow-up with new information
plan.text: If you have a new listing, a price change, or a market update, send it with one question. Do not send a plain check-in, because it gives the buyer nothing to answer.

plan.label: Later
plan.title: Call if the buyer prefers calls
plan.text: If the buyer is older or your notes say they prefer calls, call once and leave a short voicemail. Follow the voicemail with a text that says you called.

plan.label: Next week
plan.title: Send the close-out message
plan.text: If there is still no reply on the close-out date, send one message. Say you will pause the search and invite them to reply with one word to restart it.

plan.label: Monthly
plan.title: Review the tracker
plan.text: Look at which reasons came up most, and which channels got replies. Change your next routine based on what you saw, not on a guess.
